name: Color depth, pixel depth and pixel ratio
plain: Reads bits per pixel and the device pixel ratio (zoom or Retina factor).
meaning: Pixel ratio shows Retina screens and browser zoom. Together with resolution it identifies display class.

data.metric: Color depth, pixel depth and pixel ratio

limits.headline: Can see your screen's color depth and how sharp or zoomed it is
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads or you zoom.
can: Check how many real pixels sit behind each page pixel (Retina or zoom)
Notice when you zoom or drag the window to another screen
cannot: Tell zoom apart from a high density screen, since the two blend into one number
See anything beyond these two numbers

story.what_it_is: Reads how many color bits the screen has and how sharp or zoomed the display is.

marketing.name: Window.devicePixelRatio
marketing.pitch: Explains the ratio of physical screen pixels to CSS pixels, which tells a page how sharp the display is.

story.for_you: You never see the reading. It is why a site shows crisp logos on a Retina laptop and a lighter picture on an old monitor.
story.for_makers: Sites use it to send images of the right size and save data. Trackers like it because ratio plus depth plus zoom make a more unusual combination than either alone.

use_cases.example: A fashion store sends sharper photos to a phone with a ratio of 3 and plain ones to a cheap screen.
A browser game draws its canvas at full sharp resolution on a Retina screen, or at half to keep a smooth frame rate on a weak laptop.
A design tool like Figma keeps lines crisp when you zoom by matching its drawing to the screen ratio.
A tracking script combines the ratio with screen size and fonts to build a device ID without cookies.
A site team sees that 40 percent of mobile visitors have a ratio of 3 and tests for that first.
A web map loads sharper tiles on dense screens so street names stay readable.
